They would also retain fuel useful operational ability if the second fuel was unavailable. RD has recently been approved for use as a diesel replacement by many diesel-engine OEMs. This includes rail use because its physical and chemical properties are very similar to those of diesel fuel. The properties of BD are similar enough to diesel fuel for BD to be used as a direct diesel replacement without any fuel system modifications by some OEMs. Others do not yet warrant the use of 100% BD (B100) because there are some differences in materials compatibility and emissions controls compatibility. 23 3.2 BIO-OIL Bio-oils from CFP and other processes are not suitable for use as drop-in diesel fuel without further upgrading help with corrosivity, viscosity, and other properties. Some studies have looked at blending bio-oil with distillate fuels and related miscibility concerns. However, to date those studies have focused primarily on the large two-stroke engines used in marine vessels. Bio-oils have a moderate to high cetane value. However, they would require a redesigned fuel delivery system, fuel injector, and perhaps combustion geometry to be able to use bio-oil in a 4-stroke engine. Not much work has not been done to understand the emissions implications of using non- upgraded bio-oil—which would be expected to be much worse than other bio-derived diesel fuels—or how well it would work as a pilot fuel. 3.3 ETHANOL AND METHANOL Ethanol and methanol are flammable low-cetane (high-octane) alternative fuels that have higher volatility and lower lubricity than diesel fuel. They have been widely used neat or in blends with gasoline in multiple spark-ignition transportation applications. More recently, the number of methanol-fueled ships in the marine sector has increased. Ethanol and methanol are both well suited for use as the primary fuel in a dual-fuel strategy. They have been demonstrated for use in port-fuel injection applications. Some challenges for rail applications include the lower energy of methanol, to a lesser extent the larger fuel tanks ethanol would require achieving the diesel equivalent range, and different safety designs needed for fuel storage systems with flammable fuels. Methanol also has a very high latent heat of vaporization; this requires engineering solutions for port fuel injection. Methanol and ethanol dual-fuel engines have been demonstrated in both locomotive engines and marine engines; the findings of these demonstrations are relevant for locomotive engines (Argonne, 2025; Atchison, 2022; Soltic et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2018). Both fuels are relevant for spark ignition, but there have not been many studies with knock implications for larger bore engines. Cummins has shown that high-power-density spark ignition engines are possible with ethanol, but they do require additional engineering compared to a retrofit (Green Car Congress, 2014). 3.4 DIMETHYL ETHER DME is a high-cetane alternative fuel that has similar working fluid properties to propane.
